lesson.menu_title: Have You Ever… — Talking About Your Life Without Dates
lesson.menu_desc: The four words that open any conversation in English -- 37 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 6 -- Have You Ever…
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Janderson Roberto Teixeira | Lesson 6 -- Have You Ever
lesson.grammar_point: present perfect with ever and never for experience

listenings.text: Here is a small thing that changes conversations, and it costs nothing. Most of us open with what do you do, and the honest problem with that question is that it gets you a job title, and a job title is not a person. Try a different one. Have you ever, and then anything at all. Have you ever lived in another country. Have you ever worked at night. Have you ever met somebody famous. It asks about a whole life without asking for a single date, so nobody has to remember anything, and there is no wrong answer. And here is the part that surprises people. Almost everybody asks it back. You ask one question, and the conversation keeps going on its own for twenty minutes.

I put this trip off for about twenty years. Every single year there was a reason, and every reason was a good one at the time. Work, money, children, the wrong month. Then last year I stopped explaining it to myself and I booked the flight. The first two days were fine and nothing special. The highlight was the second afternoon, when I got lost looking for a museum and I found a street market instead. I stayed there until it closed. I have travelled a reasonable amount since then, and I have noticed something. I have never regretted going anywhere. I have regretted waiting, every single time.

extra_audio.text: Emma asks Janderson whether he has ever been to London before. He answers that he has been twice, but only for work. Emma asks him what he is into when he is not in an office. He says he is into old maps and that he has put off looking for twenty years. Emma tells him to go on Saturday and to get lost on purpose.

reading.rtitle: The Best Question at a Dinner Table
paras: There is one question in English that works with anybody, in any country, at any table. It is not what do you do. That one gets you a job title, and a job title tells you almost nothing about a person.

The question is have you ever. Have you ever lived abroad. Have you ever worked at night. Have you ever got lost in a city you did not know. It asks about a whole life at once, and it never asks for a date, so nobody has to remember anything and nobody can get it wrong.

That is the grammar of it, and the grammar is doing real work here. This tense exists precisely for experience with no calendar attached. The moment you say last March or in 2019, English changes the verb and you are talking about one occasion instead of a life. Both are useful. Only one of them opens a conversation.

And there is a second effect that people notice immediately. Almost everybody asks it back. You ask one question, you answer one question, and the conversation continues on its own for twenty minutes without anybody working at it. For somebody who is afraid of silence in a second language, that is not a small thing.
reading.source: Article -- a column on conversation in a language magazine
